claims.text: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy incorporating low-activation elements can serve as a structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
Tungsten has a high melting point suitable for plasma-facing applications.
Tungsten exhibits low sputter erosion under plasma-facing conditions.
A high-entropy alloy design enhances radiation resistance.
Incorporating low-activation elements into the tungsten-based RHEA reduces long-term radioactive activation.
The as-cast or additively manufactured tungsten-based RHEA has a homogeneous solid-solution microstructure.
Fusion divertor plasma-facing materials operate at temperatures of at least 1000 K while exposed to heat, hydrogen isotopes, helium, and neutrons.
Fusion exposure will produce coherent nanoprecipitates in the tungsten-based RHEA.
Fusion exposure will produce a refined, radiation-tolerant grain structure in the tungsten-based RHEA.
High configurational entropy causes coherent nanoprecipitation and grain refinement.
High-entropy mixing reduces the thermodynamic driving force for radiation-defect formation.
High-entropy mixing slows atomic diffusion.
Reduced defect-formation driving force and slower diffusion limit radiation-induced microstructural degradation.
Avoiding elements that produce long-lived radionuclides minimizes activation.
The tungsten-based RHEA will have better mechanical stability than conventional tungsten after fusion-relevant exposure.
The tungsten-based RHEA will exhibit less erosion than conventional tungsten.
The tungsten-based RHEA will retain less tritium than conventional tungsten.
The tungsten-based RHEA will have lower induced radioactive activation than conventional tungsten.
Improved mechanical stability, erosion resistance, tritium retention, and activation behavior will extend plasma-facing-component lifetime.
The balance among strength, ductility, oxidation resistance, and low activation depends on alloy composition and processing and remains to be optimized.
